subject: frostAxe
pitch:
Category: Fantasy weapon.
Subject: frost-forged battle axe.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm envisioning a frost-forged battle axe in a stylized League of Legends aesthetic—bold hand-painted shapes, glowing ice crystals, runes etched into blue-tinted steel, with fur and leather wrapping. Since it's a standalone weapon prop with no creature involved, I just need to build all the geometry through the builder with a single root joint.

I'm deciding to create one joint called "root" at the haft's base, then plant the axe upright on a small snowy stone-and-ice plinth (~0.12 height) with the axe starting at y=0 on the base. The crescent blade head will extend sideways in the X-axis rather than forward, using the extrude function oriented so the blade's outline spreads in the x-y plane while thickness runs along z—this way the axe reads properly from the front viewer's perspective, with the blade silhouette visible and the back-spike or ice crystal accent on the opposite side.

Now I'm sketching the base: an octagonal lathed plinth of dark mottled stone topped with a snow cap, surrounded by faceted glowing ice crystal cones and a few rocks, radius 0.4 and height 0.1, with the axe haft sinking slightly into it. For the haft itself, I'm planning a straight swept shape with an octagonal cross-section, slightly thicker at the middle, painted with a dark frosted wood grain, and considering steel bands as reinforcement rings along its length—possibly using thin cylinder or lathe geometry to simulate the metal bands.

For the leather grip, I'm spiraling a thin wrapped tube around the haft near its midpoint, calculating turns and pitch to get a natural wrap effect with a leather-brown tone. Since the butt of the haft is planted into the base and hidden, I'm considering skipping a separate pommel cap there, or possibly adding a small decorative ring instead to finish that transition cleanly.

Now I'm plotting the axe head's socket and blade geometry, defining the bearded crescent shape with a flaring horn and convex cutting edge as a series of coordinate points around the haft's upper section.

Continuing the outline through the bottom horn and back to the starting point near the socket, I want to make sure the path doesn't self-intersect and closes cleanly. I'll apply smoothing level 1 with sharp corner markers at the horn tips, being cautious since aggressive smoothing can fail if a cut corner crosses another edge on tight curves.

For the blade construction, I'm layering it: a base frost-blued steel layer at constant thickness with a modest bevel, then an inner icy inlay scaled slightly smaller and extruded a bit thicker, glowing pale cyan, to create that layered frozen-blade look rather than a simple edge taper.

Writing paint gradient logic...

Adding serrated icicle teeth along the blade edge and hanging shards beneath the horn, plus a cluster of crystal spikes growing off the back of the head using cone-like geometry variations for a jagged, organic ice formation.

I'm confirming the lathe can orient along an arbitrary axis, then applying glow with flat crystal colors around 0.8 strength to avoid overbrightening. For the back of the head, I'm sketching a mirrored spike fluke on the −x side with a sharp tip profile, maybe adding a crystal cluster behind it for extra detail.

Now I'm adding a top spike crystal growing from the poll, lathing an ice-tipped steel cone above the haft so total height reaches about 1.75m for a realistic 1.6m axe. I'm also working out the socket sleeve as a lathed cylinder profile positioned around y 1.2–1.52, centered on the haft with a bone-root color scheme using metal paint.

I'll also pull in glow effects from the kit, keeping the flat colour palette under 64 while letting paints handle gradients freely. For textures, I'm planning around 5-12: a glowing rune blade, a small glowing snowflake emblem disc for the badge, a fur tuft card, and a ground rune circle decal, among others like frost crack patterns and icicle cards.

Rounding out the texture set, I'm adding scattered ice-shard frost cards and small glowing four-pointed star sparkle cards floating around the head as magical motes, rendered as double-sided cards passed through the glow system.

I'm also adding a hanging tribal pennant tassel near the haft attachment using a bent double-sided card with a chevron pattern, plus leather ties, fur, and cracked-ice glow lines on the base, before moving into actually coding the builder function with its root structure.

Setting up joints and base profile...

Writing stone and snow paint logic...

Adding scattered rocks and glowing ice crystal clusters around the base, then working out a rune circle plane positioned carefully on the domed snow mound's surface.

Adding the glowing texture plane and sketching the wooden haft now, sweeping a tube along a simple two-point path with slight radius variation and a grain paint pattern for the wood color.

Now working out the spear tip geometry on top of the haft, shaping a lathed point with a slim diamond-like profile for the steel spike.

Below it, I'm lathing the socket piece that collars the shaft, giving it a flared, ringed profile with blued metal coloring, positioned so the blade centers nicely above the haft joint.

Now I'm setting up the blade extrusion with a slight bevel and thickness, then writing the paint function that shades the icy edge zones near the blade's tip using smoothstep gradients based on outline coordinates.

I'm skipping the bevel highlight idea and focusing on the inlay instead—designing a faceted ice-crystal core plus rune panel on the blade face, slightly proud of the surface with a cyan glow, and sketching out the outline points for that crystal shape.

I'm checking that the crystal outline stays within the blade's boundary at each point, confirming it fits inside the notch region. Then I'm settling on colors: a mid-ice cyan for the glowing inlay base, with brighter white rune lines layered on top for contrast.

Positioning the rune plane just above the inlay surface, sized to fit within the blade's crystal area, and sketching Elder Futhark-style rune strokes plus a small snowflake motif centered in the texture, scaled so the stroke width reads clearly at the final render size, oriented upright along the blade.

For the back fluke spike, I'm reusing the same paint function as the main blade, mapping outline coordinates so the base reads as dark steel and the tip transitions toward icy white, since the extrusion direction just flips the x-axis without needing new logic.

Now I'm adding crystal clusters erupting from the back of the poll and behind the fluke, using a lathe-based helper that builds a sharp, faceted gem shape from a small outline profile with low segment count for a crystalline look, then orienting each crystal along a direction vector from its base point.

Picking a deeper blue for the crystal gradient, then moving to the fur collar beneath the head: a ring of fur cards around y≈1.1-1.16, facing outward with a downward tilt so they hang like fringe rather than pointing up along the axis.

I'll leave the fur texture uncolored so its own tones show through rather than tinting the cards. For the grip, I'm wrapping a spiral sweep of dark leather around the haft between y 0.5 and 0.98, with a darker core underneath for depth, checking which direction the turns should wind.

Then I'm adding metal ring bands at the grip boundaries and foot using a hollow lathe profile for steel rings, leaning into a frost-warrior palette of dark iron, ice blue, and fur with a touch of gold trim for accent.

Adding gold rivet studs...

Now I'm thinking about frost crystals and icicle shards growing along the blade's edge to sell the frozen theme.

Still placing crystals...

Next I'll add a hanging tassel below the head, made of cloth-textured cards facing upward near the fur.

So I'll draw the SVG flipped, with viewBox 0 0 40 120, free swallow-tail end at y=0 and attached end at y=120, so the hanging cloth reads correctly when viewed from downstream per the doc's upside-down convention.

Since I'm avoiding mirror/flip ambiguity, I'll just make the design symmetric and apply a vertical flip, which sidesteps the question of whether it's rotated or mirrored. I'll add a slight bend and flow tilt for realism.

For the frost motes, I'll scatter around 14 small star cards randomly through a volume near the head, using cross-card framing with double-sided rendering, sizes around 0.05–0.08, and a glow of 1.0, adjusting sizing so they read clearly.

Now I'm constraining the motes to stay within a radius of 0.6 and heights between 0.4 and 1.9, skipping the frosty vine idea on the haft. For the boss crystals, I'm placing a ring of 8 crystals around radius 0.34 on the snow cap, tilting them outward with varying sizes, keeping the axe shaft clear near the center, and adding a few more crystals near the plinth's outer edge angled outward and downward.

For the rocks, I'm using flat-shaded low-poly icosahedrons with stone material, placing 6 of them at radius 0.5-0.58 between the crystals, squashed vertically and embedded so their bases sit just above the ground plane. I'm also considering carved rune glyph plates on the plinth's 8 sides instead of trying to wrap text around the rim as a decal, since that's simpler than curving text geometry.

Working through the math for positioning those rune plates against the octagonal lathe geometry, I'm computing the apothem distance at the right height so the glowing plates sit flush against each face without clipping, offsetting them slightly outward and rotating each by 22.5 degrees to align with the plinth's facets.

Actually decal is simpler and more robust here — I can conform the rune texture directly to the surface at each hit point with a slight lift, rather than computing plane orientation manually. I'll place 8 decals around the plinth at 45-degree azimuth steps, alternating rune glyphs, using a cyan rune-in-circle texture set.

Now I'm designing the rune glyph artwork: a small viewBox with stacked stroke-based glyphs (snowflake accent plus a few vertical rune marks), white strokes with rounded caps on a transparent background so the cyan inlay glow shows through the gaps. I'm also sketching a six-armed snowflake emblem for the collar band disc.

For placement, rather than tangent-plane geometry that would float near the curved socket edges, I'll use a decal applied directly onto the socket surface at the front, oriented outward with a small size, plus a mirrored decal on the back side so it wraps naturally around the curve.

Skipping the haft inscription for now. I'm considering adding frost-crack lines to the blade paint using a cellular noise pattern, blending white-blue cracks near the edges with a smoothstep falloff. For the gold accents, I'll treat the socket as painted metal with a blue-noise gradient and add separate lathe-ring geometry for gold bands rather than painting them, and I'm starting to lay out the flat color palette with entries like gold and leather tones.

Part count is modest so far around 120, but I want to push toward 180-340 by adding studs, rune plates, crystal clusters, motes, rocks, snow drifts, and icicle details—favoring quality but padding out the geometry reasonably. I'm also considering a hanging ice-crystal charm on a thin cord looped from the socket, sweeping a catmull curve from the side down to the charm.

Deciding to skip the charm since the cord would cross the fur, opting for a tassel instead. Writing the build script now...

Writing blade paint colors...

Defining STONE paint...

I'm noting it should return snow paint on upward-facing surfaces with enough noise, otherwise fall back to a patchy dark stone texture — better to build the patches generator once outside the callback rather than per-call. Snow paint itself is a mottled white-to-pale-blue texture, and I'm sketching a dark purple wood grain for the haft with a possible frost-touched variant.

I'm now setting up FUR_CORE as a mottled pale blue-gray texture and working out the lathe profiles for the stone plinth and the snow mound sitting on top of it, checking that their radii and heights line up so the snow mound's base sits correctly within the plinth's top rim.

I'll scatter a handful of flattened icosahedra as snow drifts near the rim, then build rocks the same way. For crystals, I'm writing a helper that lathes a tapered hexagonal spike shape anchored to a base point and oriented along a direction vector.

Still writing crystal helper...

I'm choosing colors from an ice palette and varying glow strength between 0.6 and 0.9 so the crystals feel internally lit rather than flat-shaded.

Shaping the barbed fluke outline...

I'm plotting out the blade outline's coordinates, checking the top and bottom horn curves don't self-intersect as they point outward from the central axis.

Now I'm sanity-checking overall proportions: blade height around 0.86m centered near y=1.36, which puts the top horn close to the spear tip at 1.81 -- so I may need to nudge the head position or shorten the spear slightly to avoid the collision, keeping total length near 1.85m.

For the haft, I'm planning segments from 0.12 to 1.56 with a grip zone around 0.5–1.0, adding bands at 0.5 and 1.0 plus a small gold pommel ring near the base at 0.2. Now I'm starting to define the texture assets, beginning with an SVG for the fur pattern.

Writing SVG fur shapes...

Then I'm designing a four-point star icon with a cyan-white glow, and a snowflake emblem on a deep blue disc with gold trim for the badge imagery, followed by runes and a concentric ground circle motif.

For the ring, I'm generating 12 rune glyphs spaced evenly around a circle using rotation transforms, plus a six-pointed star built from two overlapping triangles, and then two rune plate variants with distinct glyph paths inside rounded squares.

Still drawing the tassel shape...

For the ice shard card I'm making a pale cyan crystal with highlight, scattered randomly across the snow ring with small size, slight glow around 0.35 for a magical feel. I'm tallying up the texture list—runes, snowflake, fur, star, ground, three plate variants, tassel, and shard—landing on ten total.

Now I'm working out the random placement logic for scattering frame cards across the snow: generating angles and radii within the ring, adjusting height based on distance from center, and making sure everything stays clear of the central haft radius.

I'm placing shards only in the outer band so they don't visually clutter the ground rune, dropping to around 14 shards total. For the hanging tassel, I'm positioning it near the fur at the top, letting the cloth drape down below without colliding with the blade's lower horn.

Now I'm setting up the ring of fur tufts: 14 items tilted outward-down around the frame, with cards sized small and a flow direction angled down and flattened onto the facing plane so they naturally follow the curve. I'm adding a second ring slightly higher with rotated spacing to stagger the tufts for a fuller look.

For the collar itself, I'm defining a lathe profile that bulges out then tapers to zero near the top, giving it a soft rounded fur-wrap shape around y 1.04–1.173, with the cards layered just inside that range.

For glow effects, I'm confirming that both decal parts and lathe parts can accept the Glowing wrapper since it just needs a mesh reference.

Then I'm looping through eight azimuth positions around the plinth, finding a surface hit point at each 45-degree interval, and placing a glowing rune decal there using one of three alternating plate textures sized around 0.085 units.

I'm double-checking whether these azimuth hits land on segment vertices or face centers given the lathe's spin offset of 22.5 degrees — since the decal is surface-projected either way should look fine, though I need to check whether the 0.085-tall decal at y=0.045 actually crosses the chamfer transition in the plinth wall profile, which could cause visual distortion.

Since the wall is nearly vertical for y 0–0.06, I'm shrinking the decal to [0.07, 0.055] so it stays safely within that region, and reworking the plinth and snow profiles to be taller with a few more control points for a cleaner silhouette. I'm also repositioning the ground rune plane to sit just above the surface at radius 0.25, setting the haft base height, and adjusting the decal placement and size to match the new geometry.

For the plane orientation I'll set up with proper axis and up vectors to avoid degenerate cases. Now I'm defining the blade's extrusion geometry with its outline, position, thickness, and bevel settings for the rune glow effect.

Sorting out the OutlinePoint typing for the blade outline array, then moving to defining the decorative inlay shape with its own set of outline points and extrusion parameters...

Mapping glyph positions...

Still drawing the snowflake and rune paths...

Checking placement bounds for two more frost crystals against the blade silhouette at different y positions, then deciding to skip a horn-tip crystal since it would hide the sharp point, opting instead for icicles under the lower horn.

Now I'm placing crystal clusters near the poll at the spear base, and adding small crystals along the fluke at the back of the head, picking directions and sizes that fit each location naturally.

For the spear itself, I'm lathing it at the top of the socket with a four-sided cross-section, giving it a flat steel-blue tint rather than overcomplicating with gradients or glow.

I'm setting up a BLUED paint that mixes dark and light blue tones with noise, then adds a frosty highlight on upward-facing surfaces—good for the socket and spear. I'll define a GOLDP paint with noise-mixed bronze and warm gold tones for bands and rings, planning gold rings around the socket near the 1.18 mark.

Now I'm lathing out the socket geometry and ring details—placing thin gold rings at specific heights (like y=1.17 and y=1.50) with small hollow rectangular cross-sections, while working out the socket's taper profile with flared ends and a slimmer middle section. Still writing lathe profile...

Next I'm planning the haft's gold bands around y=0.2, 0.5, and 1.0, then setting up a leather spiral grip winding around the haft core from y=0.53 to 0.97 with eight turns, swept along a helical path with a small tube radius.

I'm deciding to skip adding a glowing translucent halo behind the axe since transparency isn't allowed, and now moving to defining the joint hierarchy starting with the root and head joints.

I'm setting up flat-shaded icosahedron geometry for the parts, then configuring the motes effect with 16 randomly scattered star-shaped cards that get a glow pass applied. I'm also wiring up the fur cards using the ring's joints and items, then moving on to generating the rocks loop.

Writing rock placement code...

Adding plinth edge crystals around the outer radius with interleaved angles, then verifying the lowest rocks sit just barely below y=0 which is fine, and confirming overall model height comes out to about 2 units.

Now I'm writing SVG markup for a decorative ground ring with rotated crystal-spike glyphs repeated every 30 degrees around a circle...

Still refining the frames and tassel positioning...
